title: mutual funds vs the plot back home
slides:
A dad saw his son's portfolio and said sell half, buy a plot back home. He wasn't being dumb. He was being smart.
Swipe to read →

I used to think this was old people being scared of risk. It isn't.
A 27-year-old in Bangalore has put everything into SIPs for four years. The portfolio keeps growing. He's proud.

He tells his parents. He's expecting at least a "wah beta".
Instead dad goes quiet. He says the whole thing could vanish overnight. Buy a plot back home.

Try to win this with a returns chart and you will lose. Every time. Because dad isn't arguing about returns.
A plot has a boundary wall. Relatives drive past it. Your chacha knows where it is.

It comes up when your cousin's rishta is discussed. It's wealth the town can verify.
Your Groww screen? Nobody knows it exists except you.
But the real thing underneath isn't showing off either.

In Indian families, whoever owns the assets makes the decisions. Always been this way.
The house is in papa's name. The land is in papa's name. So papa decides where you study and who you marry.

Your portfolio is the first serious money in the family that doesn't need papa's name. Or his permission.
Which is why the counter-offer is never "invest a bit less". It's always a plot.

A plot pulls the money back where the family can see it. Back to the town you left.
It's also a reason to keep coming back. You'll go see it, pay someone, sign papers.

So the market isn't the risk your parents are worried about.
They're looking at the first generation whose money and decisions don't pass through home anymore. The scary part isn't you'll lose the money.

It's that you won't need them to keep it.
And if you're building in fintech, this is your real competition. Not other apps. A plot their father can drive past on a Sunday.

title: the eldest child
slides:
There's a generation of 30-year-olds in India with good jobs, quietly asking strangers online if they're finally allowed to spend on themselves.
Swipe to read →

I'm only half joking. Once the eldest starts earning, the bills just appear.
Papa's old loan from the village moneylender, at some crazy interest rate. Their own education loan too.

Then the younger one's college fees. Mummy's hospital bills. And eventually both parents' entire retirement.
Nobody sits them down and asks. It just starts around 23 and never officially stops.

Because nobody asked, there's no clear end. No last EMI. No "okay beta, you've done enough, go live your life."
So you get 29 and 30 year olds asking online if they're finally allowed to spend on themselves.

Grown adults with good jobs, asking for permission. That honestly tells you everything about how this works.
The family isn't evil here. That's what makes it so hard. They're genuinely grateful.

Every relative hears how much the eldest has done. But that praise is exactly what keeps the whole thing running.
You can't walk away from being the pillar of the family.

After a few years it stops being something you do. It becomes who you are. Buying yourself something nice starts to feel like stealing.
And nobody does the maths on what comes next.

The eldest spends their whole twenties paying for their parents' old age. Which means they're not saving for their own.
Late marriage. Late house. No real retirement fund of their own.

So by 60 they're exactly where their parents were. And guess who they'll need? Their own eldest kid.
It's basically a loan every generation takes from the next one.

The interest gets paid in someone's twenties. Everyone keeps saying India's young population is its biggest advantage.
But in millions of homes that dividend is already spent. Paid off quietly by someone nobody ever asked.

title: India's real luxury market isn't fashion or cars It's privacy. Gated c
slides: India's real luxury market isn't fashion or cars It's privacy. Gated communities, private hospitals, business class, VIP darshan. The wealthiest Indians are paying to avoid other Indians. That's the ultimate status signal.

A 3 crore flat in a gated community isn't about Italian marble, it's about a guard at the gate who decides who gets in. Business class isn't about legroom, it's about a curtain between you and 200 strangers. A R15,000 private hospital consultation isn't about better healthcare, it's about not sitting in a room with 60 people waiting for one doctor.

We live in one of the most densely populated, most chaotic, most sensorially overwhelming countries on the planet. And when you grow up surrounded by noise and crowds and people everywhere in trains, in markets, in your own home with 12 relatives, the ultimate dream isn't a bigger house or a faster car. It's silence, space, and the ability to exist without being pushed, stared at, or judged by other Indians.

We don't talk about this because it sounds elitist, but every person reading this who has money is already spending on it. You just don't call it luxury, you call it quality of life or safety or good locality or premium experience. Strip away the euphemisms and what you're paying for is distance from the crowd.

The brands that win next won't sell louder, flashier, more visible products. They'll sell invisibility, exclusivity, and the promise that you'll never have to share your experience with someone who didn't pay the same price. In a country of 1.4 billion people, the scarcest resource isn't gold or land or time, it's personal space. And the people who have money will pay almost anything to protect it.

title: Imagine you're in a massive auditorium with 362 million Indians. Every
slides: Imagine you're in a massive auditorium with 362 million Indians. Every age. Every income level. Every social class. And one by one, each person gets to walk on stage and show off ONE thing about their life.

The billionaire shows his Rolls Royce. The college student shows her new iPhone. The maid shows her daughter's wedding. The startup founder shows his "unicorn" announcement. The retired uncle shows his Goa vacation. Everyone watching. Everyone comparing. Everyone feeling something. This is Instagram.

Here's what makes Instagram different from every social space in history: In real life, you only compare yourself to people in your circle. Your classmates. Your colleagues. Your neighbors. Your relatives. Maybe 50-100 people total. On Instagram, your comparison group just became 1 million people. The delivery guy compares himself to Ranveer Allahbadia. The teacher compares herself to Komal Pandey. The CA compares himself to startup founders.

The 725,000/month guy watches: Millionaire's Maldives trip Friend's new car Colleague's promotion Influencer's brand deal His brain does this: "Everyone's winning except me." "I'm 28 and still here." "What am I doing wrong?" "Maybe I should take that loan for the car."

The Most Brutal Part: In real life: Poor people knew they were poor. Rich people knew they were rich. Middle class knew they were middle class. Everyone stayed in their lane because they couldn't see other lanes. On Instagram: Everyone sees everyone. The lanes disappeared.

Result: Middle class feels poor (comparing to rich) Rich feel inadequate (comparing to richer) Poor feel invisible (nobody's watching their stage performance) For the first time in history, every social class is forced to watch every other social class perform their best life. And it's making everyone miserable. This is the psychological experiment nobody consented to.

But here's where it gets darker. That 725,000/month guy watching everyone else's highlight reel? He doesn't just feel poor. He feels like he's falling behind. And when you feel like you're falling behind, you don't save money. You spend it. To catch up.

Result: in 2024. India's personal loan market hit 710 lakh crores Credit card debt is at an all-time high. Buy Now Pay Later is exploding. People aren't spending more because they're earning more. They're spending more because they're comparing more.

title: Dhurandhar 2 is almost 4 hours long. And people are sitting through ev
slides: Dhurandhar 2 is almost 4 hours long. And people are sitting through every single minute of it. That tells you something important about how cinema is quietly changing in India

Let's be honest. Four hours is a lot to ask of someone. You're buying a ticket, finding parking, dealing with a crowded multiplex, and then sitting in a dark room for the length of two average Bollywood films back to back. By every conventional rule of theatrical distribution, Dhurandhar 2 should not be working.But it is.

Part of it is simply that the film is really good. Aditya Dhar shot 7 hours of footage across India and Thailand. Rather than cut it to 2-2.5 hours like every other director would have, he split it into two films. Part 1 and Part 2 and each is nearly four hours long. He trusted that if the story was strong enough, the clock wouldn't matter. He was right.

But here's the insight nobody is talking about. Dhurandhar 1 wasn't structured like a movie. It was structured like a TV series broken into chapters. Each chapter lands like an episode. There's a cliffhanger, a revelation, a shift in tone, and then the next chapter begins before you've processed the last one. People aren't sitting in the theatre for 4 hours. They're binge-watching in the dark. It felt less like watching a film and more like finishing 6 episodes of something you couldn't stop.

This is what Netflix and Prime have actually done to Indian audiences. They didn't kill the theatrical experience. They rewired how people consume narrative. An entire generation now has the stamina for long-form storytelling. 8-episode seasons. 10- episode series. 60 minutes per episode, no interval. Dhurandhar figured out how to bring that muscle into the cinema hall.

Every filmmaker complains that OTT has ruined the audience's attention span. Aditya Dhar looked at the same audience and said actually, they can sit for four hours if you earn every minute of it. The runtime isn't the problem. The pacing is.

The real insight here isn't about Dhurandhar. It's about what Indian audiences are ready for. They'll pay for a ticket, sit through four hours, skip the interval samosas, and not check their phone if you give them something that feels like it's going somewhere. Chapter by chapter. Episode by episode.

title: There's something bizarre about Indian consumer behaviour. • • • I kno
slides: There's something bizarre about Indian consumer behaviour. I know a guy who spent 71,00,000 on a phone and then spent 45 minutes last month looking for a cracked APK because he didn't want to pay 799 for an app. Another friend of mine bought a 73 lakh Royal Enfield but refuses to pay 7500 a month for Spotify, so he just sits through the ads like it's nothing. And every uncle who has spent 715 lakhs on his daughter's wedding has also stood in a sabzi mandi for 30 minutes fighting with a vendor over

Same people, same wallets, and completely opposite behaviour depending on what they're buying. We don't buy products. We buy proof. That iPhone isn't really a phone, it's proof that you've made it. That Enfield isn't transport, it's proof that you're not like everyone else on the road. That wedding isn't a ceremony, it's proof that your family has standing in the community. But Spotify Premium? Nobody knows you have it. That 799 app sits invisibly on your phone where no one will ever see it. And nobody at the mandi is judging how much you paid for your vegetables.

So the actual rule is this. Indians will happily pay a premium for consumption that other people can see, and will fight to the death to avoid paying for consumption that nobody can see. And once you notice it, you start seeing it everywhere. Zara is packed every single weekend because a ‹ 3,000 shirt is something people will notice, but barely anyone in this country pays 7500 a year for a news subscription because nobody knows you have one. Starbucks has a line out the door because a 7400 coffee can go on Instagram, while meditation apps convert at 0.2% because your mental health, at 71,500 a year, is invisible to everyone but you.

My favourite example of all. people will buy an 780,000 sofa for the living room because guests will sit on it, and then sleep on a 10-year-old mattress in the bedroom because nobody ever goes in there.

There's a second layer to this that took me even longer to understand. We are terrified of being taken advantage of, and it's not really about the money at all. It's the fear of looking like a fool, of paying for something that everyone else somehow got for free. This is why nobody ever admits they paid for Tinder Gold, why every person you know "got a discount" on everything they've ever bought, and why perfectly sane people will spend two hours hunting for a coupon code that saves them F100. The shame of overpaying is bigger than the joy of owning, every single time.

And the flip side of that fear is that we're genuinely, openly proud of getting things free or cheap. "Arre, let me just find it on Amazon during the sale." "Why pay for it when you can download it or borrow it or share someone's password?" This isn't frugality, and I don't think it ever was. This is sport. Getting a discount is a social achievement that you tell your friends about at dinner. Paying full price is a social failure that you either hide or lie about.

So if you're building anything in India, you can skip the surveys and the focus groups, because there's really only one question that matters. Would your customer be embarrassed or proud to tell their friends they bought your product? If the answer is embarrassed, you're selling invisible value, and that's the hardest thing to sell in this country. If the answer is proud, you're selling visible status, and half your marketing is already done for you.

title: People don't move to Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune etc, just for the job.
slides: People don't move to Bangalore, Hyderabad, Pune etc, just for the job. They move to become someone their hometown wouldn't recognize.

The job is the excuse. The anonymity is the reason. In your hometown, every purchase is witnessed. Every relationship is reported back. Every life choice gets an opinion from someone your parents know. The surveillance isn't malicious. It's just constant. And after 22 years of it, a city where nobody knows your family name feels less like a relocation and more like oxygen.

This is why Bangalore, Pune, Hyderabad grew the way they did and why Delhi and Chennai didn't produce the same cultural shift. Delhi pulls people who want proximity to power. Chennai pulls people who want proximity to family. Mumbai pulls people who want proximity to fame. But Bangalore pulled people who specifically wanted distance. From something. The city became a collection of deliberate escapees, and that changes everything about how people live, spend, and decide.

The most radical thing about Bangalore isn't the startups or the pubs or the weather. All they ask is your learn a little of their language and respect their culture. In return you get one of the only cities in India where you're allowed to just be whoever you showed up as. No one judges you here. No context required. No explanation owed. No committee deciding if you belong. In a country that has opinions about everything, that is not a small thing. That is everything.

title: The Millennial Silence Problem Why one of the most experienced generat
slides: The Millennial Silence Problem Why one of the most experienced generation on the internet stopped talking and what it's costing all of us. Swipe to read - →

Millennials are online more than ever. Scrolling at 2am, saving posts they'll never revisit, consuming reels endlessly. But they've stopped posting. Stopped writing, stopped making videos, stopped sharing what they know from years of actually doing the work. An entire generation's worth of lived experience, pattern recognition, and hard-won nuance is sitting in people's heads doing nothing for anyone.

In that silence, Gen Z took over the internet. Not just the trends and aesthetics, the opinions. The frameworks. The "here's how the world works" content. Career advice, financial advice, relationship advice, industry explainers. They picked up the mic enthusiastically, confidently, and often without the context that only comes from having lived through enough cycles to know what you don't know.

A 22-year-old with 8 months of work experience makes a confident video titled "Why your manager is gaslighting you" gets 4 million views. Meanwhile a 37-year-old who's managed teams for a decade, navigated three downturns, hired and fired and been fired, has genuine scar tissue from real leadership mistakes, watches the video, thinks "this is so untrue," and says nothing. Posts nothing and does nothing. Everyone loses. The creator never gets a thoughtful counterpoint. What's worse is the audience builds mental models from a sample size of one.

There's a term for what's happening and it's called premature authority. Speaking with the certainty of an expert from the experience base of a beginner. Financial advice from people who've never lived through a real crash with actual money at stake. Career advice from people who've had two jobs. Parenting content from people who don't have children, repackaging attachment theory PDFs as lived wisdom. The production quality is high. The confidence is high. What's missing is the depth that only comes from having been wrong enough times.

Algorithms don't measure depth of experience. They measure engagement. A confident, slightly provocative take from someone with zero context will outperform a nuanced "well, it depends" take from someone who's actually seen both sides every single time. And millennials know this. Which is partly why they don't post. They think "my take is too complicated for a reel." So they say nothing. And the reductive version wins by default.

This isn't theoretical. People are making career decisions based on Linkedin posts written by people who've had one job. Financial decisions based on threads from people who started investing in a bull market and think that's just how it works. Worldviews about politics, health, business, relationships all shaped disproportionately by people who haven't had the reps yet. And the people who HAVE had the reps are right there in the audience, rolling their eyes, saying nothing.

Let me be clear this is a millennial abdication problem. Somewhere around 2018-2019, millennials collectively decided that posting was cringe. That it was for "influencers." They retreated into group chats and dinner table rants that go nowhere. They became the generation of "l could write a whole post about this" but never does. By stepping back, they didn't opt out of the attention economy. They handed the microphone to whoever was willing to pick it up.

title: There's a generation in India earning 30 LPA that genuinely feels poor
slides: There's a generation in India earning 30 LPA that genuinely feels poor. And I know how that sounds. 30 lakhs is top 1% of this country. Our parents would've called relatives. But this person opens a home buying app, sees a 3BHK in Indiranagar for 2.8 crores, does the EMI math in their head, and closes the app.

See, our parents had a ladder. Job, flat, car, kids, retirement. Boring, but every step existed. You could stand on it. That ladder is broken now. In 2005 a flat cost around 4-5 years of a decent salary. Today it's 12-15 years. Salaries went up 3x, property went up 10x.

The flat was never just a flat. It was proof to your parents, to yourself that you'd made it. And when the flat becomes impossible, that need for proof doesn't disappear. It just looks for a smaller vehicle. Psychologists actually have a name for this compensatory consumption. When the real goal gets blocked, people buy symbols of it instead. And the substitute has to signal the same thing. They buy the iPhone Pro Max. The boutique gym. The expensive Ramen dinner that obviously goes on Instagram.

Which explains so much of what you see around you. Your friend who "can't save" but has AirPods Max. The 2k coffee subscriptions everywhere in Indiranagar. Everyone has an aunty about it "this generation doesn't know how to save, lifestyle inflation" ", all that. But it's not indiscipline. The money that would've been a down payment is still doing exactly what a down payment does - buying the feeling of having arrived.

And I don't think this generation is being irrational. Honestly the opposite. They looked at a game that became unwinnable, and instead of grinding for 15 years towards a step that doesn't exist, they moved the game somewhere it could actually be played. The aspiration didn't die. It just changed address. So yeah, judge the iPhone if you want. But you might be looking at the most rational financial behaviour in the country right now.

title: India went from "therapy is for crazy people" to "therapy is cool" in
slides: India went from "therapy is for crazy people" to "therapy is cool" in about four years. Somewhere in that jump, an entire generation learned the language of mental health without doing the work of mental health.

The vocabulary arrived first. Trauma. Triggers. Toxic people. Emotional unavailability. Boundaries. Healing. Attachment Styles. These words entered group chats, Instagram captions, and dinner table conversations faster than any awareness campaign could have planned. And for a while, it felt like progress.

But there's a difference between knowing the words and doing the thing the words describe. Knowing that avoidance is a trauma response doesn't mean you stop avoiding. Knowing that you have attachment issues doesn't mean you've worked through them. Knowing the name of the wound is not the same as cleaning it.

Therapy in India became an aesthetic before it became a practice. The person who posts about "healing" has had just two therapy sessions and stopped when it got uncomfortable. Everyone spoke about therapy but most of them didn't actually go for therapy

Real therapy is uncomfortable in a way that doesn't make good content. You sit with someone for an hour and they ask you questions you don't want to answer. You leave feeling worse, not better. You go home and think about something your mother said in 1997 and feel an emotion you don't have an Instagram caption for. You cancel next week's session because it's too much. You come back anyway..

The cruelest part is what this does to the people around them. A person armed with therapy vocabulary but not therapy depth is genuinely more difficult to be in a relationship with than someone who never encountered any of it. They can name your behavior patterns before you can. They can exit conversations by calling them triggering. They can frame their own avoidance as self-protection and yours as toxicity. The vocabulary, without the work, becomes a weapon with a wellness label on it.

Real therapy costs something. Time, money, and more than anything else, the specific discomfort of looking at yourself clearly for an extended period without looking away. Most people got as far as learning the language and decided that was enough. A generation that can diagnose everyone around them but can't sit with their own discomfort for more than ten minutes. That's not a mental health revolution.

title: The free AI year is ending for a whole generation
slides:
Everyone built their workday around free ChatGPT and Claude. This month, ChatGPT's free year ends and Rs 399 a month starts. Who's ready?
Swipe to read →

The free year was never a gift. It's the first half of a very old plan.
The numbers are already set. You just haven't looked at the second half yet.

ChatGPT Go was free for a year from November 2025. Around November 2026, the auto-billing quietly starts at Rs 399 a month.
Nobody circled that date on a calendar. The app already did.

And the free plan on Claude was never meant to be the plan.
It's there so you hit the limit in the middle of a deadline. Then you upgrade without thinking twice.

You know exactly who I mean.
The analyst who hasn't written a cold email from scratch in a year. The student whose every assignment opens in a chat box.
The bill just hasn't landed yet.

This is the oldest playbook in India.
Give something away until a whole country builds its day around it. Let the habit set. Then put a price on it.
The free part is never the business.

But the usual version of this was a service. You could downgrade the plan. You could take the bus.
This one is different. It stopped being a thing you use.

It's how you write, study and work now.
Walking away doesn't mean cancelling an app. It means relearning how to do your own job without the thing that's been doing half of it.

The next hook is out. Google is giving Indian students a free year of its AI Pro plan. It catches them while they're broke and forming the habit.
None of this was about the price. It was about renting your thinking by the month.
note: Edited by hand per owner: name ChatGPT and Claude; fixed two lines broken by the polish step.

title: Portfolio Flex
slides:
Park a new car outside and the first comment is 'what's the EMI?' Post a fifty-lakh portfolio and nobody asks a thing.
Swipe to read →

The green number, the little arrow, a caption about discipline.
Posted on close friends. Quietly dropped on LinkedIn.
Ten lakhs. Twenty-five. Fifty. The car quietly stopped doing this job.

You post the new car. The first comment is from a cousin asking what the on-road price was.
The second one, in your head, is everyone wondering about the EMI.

A car invites questions you don't want. How long is the loan? What's the down payment? How are you managing all this?
The thing is sitting in the parking. Anyone can do the math.

The portfolio screenshot has none of that problem.
Nobody can see the salary behind it. Nobody knows if your parents topped it up. Nobody asks how many years it took.

A Groww or Zerodha screen only ever invites one reaction. Respect.
Maybe a "how did you build this" in the DMs.
That's a very different comment section than the car post gets.

And the format rewards you for being early with your own money.
The milestone posts are rarely just a number now. They come wrapped in a story.
A loan finally cleared. Years of SIPs. A hard patch survived.

Often it's genuinely hard-won. But it's also doing the exact work the car used to do.
It's saying look where I am now.
Watch the comments and you'll see the flex quietly working.

Someone jokes about finally clearing the credit card bill for a MacBook they bought to study on and mostly watch movies on.
Someone prepping for CAT, scoring badly in mocks, asks which college tier you did your MBA from.

Nobody's rude. But everyone is measuring their own number against yours.
The car at least gave something back. A ride, a reason to visit.
The portfolio gives nothing. All the status, nothing anyone can verify.

title: Manufactured Bestseller
slides:
Five identical phone cases. Same seller. Same photos. Every one crowned "Bestseller." The word officially means nothing now.
Swipe to read →

You read it as a verdict from millions of buyers. It's closer to a highlighter.
Open any category. Phone cases, shoes, protein, kurtas. You'll see five near-identical listings. Same seller, same photos, slightly different lighting.

And every single one is wearing a "Bestseller" or "Trending" badge.
If all five are the best-selling one, the word stopped meaning anything. A real bestseller is one per shelf. This is a sticker printed in bulk.

Here's why it exists.
People don't buy what's good. People buy what other people already bought.
The badge is a shortcut for your brain. Someone else did the thinking. You're safe. Add to cart.

The platform knows that badge makes you click faster than any discount. So why wait for the sales to actually happen?
That's the quiet switch. Consensus sells faster than quality. So they manufacture it.

A product gets the tag so it sells more. Then it sells more because it has the tag.
You're standing in a line that was drawn around you after you got there.

And it works on me too, which is the annoying part.
I check three apps for a price difference. I read way too many reviews. Then a tiny coloured label does what the whole comparison was supposed to do.

"Bestseller" bypasses the part of me that was being careful.
So if you're buying, treat the badge like packaging, not proof. It tells you what someone wanted you to click. Not what held up over time.

And if you're building a brand in India, the lesson is older than any app.
The crowd doesn't follow quality. It follows the look of a crowd. Someone figured out you can just paint that on.

title: QR Code Wallpaper
slides:
Five faded QR stickers sit on your kirana counter. Fintechs spent crores on IPL jerseys. Guess which one you actually scanned today?
Swipe to read →

Think about where you actually see these brands. Not on TV during a match.
At the sabzi cart, holding a bag of tomatoes. The vendor points at a laminated square taped to the scale.
That's the moment of truth.

Paytm over PhonePe over GPay. Corners peeling, half of them faded.
You're paying, you're deciding, and the logo that happens to be sitting there gets the sale. Without saying a word.

The auto stand has it. The chaiwala has it.
The medical shop counter has three of them, fighting for space next to the discount strips.
You've scanned every one of them.

You probably couldn't tell me which app you used this morning.
You just pointed your phone at whatever square was clearest. Then you moved on and never thought about it again.

This should make every brand team uncomfortable.
Trust for these apps got built through sheer repetition, at the exact spot where money changes hands. Not through a campaign. Nobody budgeted for it.

Just the same logo, in the same place, a hundred times a week, until scanning it feels like second nature.
That's not advertising. That's becoming furniture, and furniture always wins.

And the vendor keeps all five stickers up for a reason. Whichever app the customer trusts, there it is.
He's not loyal to anyone. He just wants the payment to go through.

That messy pile is the most honest thing in Indian fintech. No app actually won.
They all just agreed to share one sticker-covered counter. Meanwhile brands keep spending on what people can see.

The jersey, the match, the big logo. The thing that converts is a peeling sticker.
If you're building for India, be present the second someone pays. Everything else is reach you'll stand in a meeting and fail to measure.

title: The Sale That Never Ends
slides:
I'm done pretending. That 'two hours left' timer on Swiggy has been running for two years straight. Nobody believes it anymore.
Swipe to read →

Open Myntra on a random Tuesday in April. Open it again in June. The sale is still running.
There was never a reason for it. It just never actually ended.

Swiggy and Zomato do the same thing. There's a little flash banner. Two hours left, order now.
You've seen that same timer for months now. So nobody really believes it anymore.

Everyone shopping on these apps has quietly figured it out. Nobody pays the first price anymore.
You add the shirt to the bag and wait. You hover over the food order and wait.

Something inside you knows a coupon is coming. A "use code" is coming.
Paying full price now feels like you missed a step. Like everyone else knows something you don't.

Here's the funny part. The brands did this to themselves.
They were so scared of an empty cart that they put a discount on everything, forever. They trained you to wait.

And now they're trapped. The day Myntra shows a real full price with no sale, your brain reads it as a price hike.
They can't ever go back up. The discount became the floor.

So the discount isn't a gift. It's just the number they decided to sell at. The MRP is basically fiction now.
You're paying the real price and being told you're a genius for finding it.

This is the quiet problem under every festive sale this season. The Big This, the End of That, the midnight deals.
When the offer runs all year, the festive one lands flat.

There's no urgency left to sell. You burned it being on sale every single week.
The discount isn't a lever anymore. It's just the resting state. Charging what something actually costs might be the most expensive thing these apps gave away for free.

title: Open to work, because of AI
slides:
Housing.com cut 300. IBM cut 100. Same day, same reason: AI did it. Why did two companies pick the exact same word?
Swipe to read →

Costs are restructuring you. AI is just the word that sounds better on LinkedIn.
Indian startup layoffs crossed 4,500 in eight months. Nobody says we overhired in 2021. They say AI.

Livspace let go of nearly 1,000 people. Reporters framed it as AI-driven restructuring.
Like a tool walked in on Monday and quietly did everyone's job over the weekend. Nobody says the funding dried up.

I've sat in enough meetings to know how a sentence gets chosen.
A company can say it cut costs and these roles went first. Or it can say it's becoming AI-native.

Same 300 people walking out. But one version makes investors nervous.
The other makes you sound ahead of the curve. Same decision, different sentence. Guess which one goes in the post.

This actually bothers me. The person laid off now carries that story too.
If the company says AI did it, they sit there wondering if they're the one the machine replaced.

It's not about their work anymore. It's about a word a leadership team picked because it reads cleaner.
And it's a convenient word. AI takes no blame. You can't be angry at a spreadsheet.

'Automation replaced the role' closes the conversation faster than 'the numbers didn't work.'
So that's the one they reach for. You can announce it long before any automation does it.

The stated reason and the real reason are rarely the same sentence. This year they've drifted further apart.
So read the next layoff and separate the two. Ask what the number was. Ask what the headline was.

title: Fresher Hiring In IT Just Collapsed 80%
slides:
IT firms once hired 600,000 freshers a year. Now it's about 120,000. The one job your parents swore was safe just cracked.
Swipe to read →

Look at the drop. Fresher intake fell from a peak of 600,000 in FY22 to about 120,000 in FY25, going by Xpheno.
That's roughly 80% gone. Not a bad quarter. The whole floor moving.

This was the plan papa and chacha agreed on without a single argument. Science stream, B.Tech, a service company, stable salary by 22.
The one path nobody debated at dinner, because everyone knew it worked.

Now look who's cutting. Wipro trimmed its fresher guidance to 7,500 to 8,000.
Oracle cut around 10,000 India jobs, the terminations sent by email at 6 AM. Qualcomm is doing its own round.

The ones still technically hired are stuck in the worst place. Nearly a thousand at Tech Mahindra are waiting on joining letters.
Over 200 Wipro recruits had onboarding deferred. Not rejected, not working.

Just a boy at home holding an offer that means nothing yet. Telling relatives he's joining soon.
And the exact thing that made this career feel safe is the thing killing it now.

It was safe because they hired in bulk. Thousands of freshers for repetitive, entry-level work.
That bulk is exactly what AI restructuring eats first. The safety was the vulnerability the whole time.

And the desks are getting more crowded. Over 12,700 people who went abroad came back this year.
Loaded with AI and cloud skills. Now competing for the same shrinking set of chairs.

And the cruel bit is who absorbs it. Not the parents who picked the path.
The 22-year-old who scored the way he was told, and still explains a gap year he didn't choose.

So the real shift isn't 25,000 to 35,000 jobs in 2026. It's that the one career families treated as risk-free is now just a bet.
If you're a parent, you can't hand a child one safe answer anymore.

title: An ad got memed before the campaign even finished running
slides:
JioStar made a Kohli-Rohit ad. The internet renamed it 'Ro-Ko' within days. And JioStar quietly won. I know how backwards that sounds.
Swipe to read →

Within days everyone called JioStar's new film the Ro-Ko ad. But fans didn't invent that nickname off the ad. They'd been calling Rohit and Kohli Ro-Ko for ages. The brand picked up a joke already lying there.
The film dropped on 7 October. Kohli ribs Rohit for saying woh instead of naming anyone. They sign off with desh ka sawaal hai, maza toh aayega. All timed right before the Sri Lanka ODIs.
Then the internet did what it does. The Ro-Ko tag was everywhere. Rohit said whenever it plays on TV they look at each other and laugh. People want masala, so there's your masala.
Marketers quietly know this one. You've been watching these two most of your life. You have opinions about both of them. You've argued about them at every family lunch for years.
The brand isn't creating that affection. It's renting it, then putting its logo at the end. In almost any other category, your campaign getting renamed by the audience is a small disaster.

You spent weeks on a line. The internet tossed it for its own joke.
Here it's the opposite. JioStar didn't lose the message to the Ro-Ko joke. It built the ad on top of one fans had already made.
The fastest way for a campaign to travel is to not fully own it. Give people something half-finished. Let them bend it into their own version. That's exactly what JioStar did here.
Cricket gets this for free, because the love is already pre-loaded. Everyone else has to earn the affection first. Then they hope the audience even bothers to remix it at all.

title: Nobody's Buying The iPhone In Cash Anymore
slides:
India's best-selling phone costs more than most Indians earn in a month. So how is everyone affording it?
Swipe to read →

Over 4% of every phone sold in India right now is an iPhone 17.
Nobody paid ₹99,900. They paid ₹8,667 a month. And told themselves that's different.

During Big Billion Days the iPhone 17 dropped from ₹99,900 to around ₹77,999. You needed the right bank card.
But the discount isn't what moved it. The no-cost EMI did. Six months, nine months, start at ₹8,667.

A phone that costs most people more than a month's salary suddenly reads like a Swiggy order. Just spread across a year.
The sticker price disappears. Your brain only sees the monthly number.

₹8,667 feels fine. You can do ₹8,667. What's ₹8,667 next to a salary.
You never add it up. Because the day you do, you're holding a phone that cost you a month of work.

And it's not just phones. Indians spent ₹23.62 lakh crore on credit cards last year. Up almost 12%.
12.16 crore cards in circulation now.
People got comfortable paying for today's thing with next month's money.

The funny part is nobody feels reckless doing it. No-cost EMI even sounds responsible.
You're being smart. You're using the offer. You'd be a fool to pay upfront. That's the story you tell yourself.

So the phone, the TV, the vacation all become ₹8,667 a month. Twelve little numbers that each look harmless.
And then the 2nd of every month arrives. Every one of them hits at once.

This is what the festive sale actually sells now. Not the discount. The permission to not think about the real price.
The brand that wins isn't the one with the best phone. It's the one that made ₹99,900 feel like ₹8,667.

title: Groceries Got Cheaper, Phones Didn't
slides:
India just decided a scooter is a basic need. The phone you run your whole life on? Still a luxury.
Swipe to read →

GST 2.0's full month showed up in the data. Food inflation went deeper negative, to -5.02%, the fifth month running.
Cooking oil, vegetables, fruit, all down. The whole index came in at 0.25%.

Small cars and two-wheelers went from 28% tax to 18%. Two-wheeler sales jumped almost 52% in the first full month after.
Drop the price, people show up. No surprise there.

Then the GST Council met on October 8. The phone industry asked for the tax to drop to 5%. The Council kept it at 18%.
That's where phones have sat since April 2020. Six and a half years.

A tax slab isn't just a number. It's the government telling you what counts as a basic need.
Dal, basic. A scooter, now basic. Your phone sits on the same shelf as show-off stuff.

Which is funny. Try getting through one normal day without it.
Your salary lands there. Your rent goes out from there. UPI, the doctor, your boss's 9pm message, the bus ticket, the bank.

The phone stopped being a gadget years ago. It's the counter where your whole life runs.
And the higher slab hits hardest the people with the least room to spare.

The delivery guy whose income lives inside an app. The woman running her shop off a QR code on the wall.
For them the phone isn't a want. It's the job itself.

When something gets held at the higher slab, read it as the government's quiet opinion of you.
It decided the phone is something you want, not something you need. Everyone holding one twelve hours a day knows that's backwards.

title: Gold Hit ₹1.5 Lakh And Nobody Stopped Buying It
slides:
Gold just hit a record ₹1,50,300 for 10 grams. Everyone expected Dhanteras buying to collapse. The shops are packed. The bills just got smaller.
Swipe to read →

People are still walking into the shop. They're just walking out with a lot less.
Nobody sits down and calculates returns on Dhanteras gold. They never did.
So what happens when the price jumps this high?

Dhanteras is on November 6 this year. Buying gold that day was never an investment decision. It's an obligation.
You buy because papa bought. Because his papa bought. Because not buying feels like tempting something.
So you still buy. Just differently.

That's what jewellers are seeing right now. The shop is full. Footfall is holding up fine.
But the grams per customer have dropped sharply. Same number of people. Much smaller purchases.
You can watch it happen at the counter.

The coin became a lighter coin. The necklace became a thin chain.
The gift became a pendant you can barely feel in your hand.
The buying didn't stop. It just got divisible. And you can see exactly where it went.

Lightweight jewellery everyone can wear, not store. Digital gold in tiny amounts on an app.
Gold ETFs sitting in a demat account nobody at Diwali will ever see.
The buying just spread out. But here's what nobody says out loud.

The gold was never fully about the gold. It was about proving, once a year, that the family is doing okay.
So when the price hits a record, you don't skip the proof. You just shrink the quantity.
The receipt still exists either way.

This is the thing with Indians and anything witnessed. The act matters more than the amount.
A visible coin beats an invisible SIP.
The jewellers figured it out. They're not selling you gold. They're selling you the ritual, at whatever price the year hands you.
